summaries.example: Imagine a class choosing rules for sharing art supplies. One rule says, “Take whatever you want whenever it helps you.” Another says, “Ask first, share fairly, and make an exception to prevent a serious problem.” The second rule may work better because it builds trust, is easier to learn, and usually helps more people, even though following it might not give the best result in every single moment.
summaries.summary: Rule consequentialism is a way of thinking about morality. It says that we should choose moral rules by asking which rules would have the best overall results when people accept, learn, and follow them. The theory is different from simply calculating the result of every single action. A rule such as “do not steal” may usually protect trust and security, even if stealing would sometimes seem to help in one particular situation. Full rule consequentialism uses consequence-based rules in three areas: deciding which acts are wrong, deciding how people should make choices, and deciding when blame, praise, guilt, or punishment are appropriate. The theory also asks what “good” means. Some philosophers focus on pleasure and avoiding pain. Others include fulfilled desires, friendship, knowledge, achievement, autonomy, fairness, justice, or equality. These ideas can pull in different directions. A simple rule code may be easier to teach and follow than a huge code filled with exceptions. Yet a code must also explain how to handle people who do not learn or follow the rules, and when preventing a disaster can justify breaking an ordinary rule. Critics ask whether rule consequentialism becomes the same as action-by-action consequentialism, becomes inconsistent, or blindly worships rules. Supporters reply that rules are selected partly because public acceptance, trust, simple teaching, and reliable cooperation can produce better long-term results.
key_ideas: Some moral theories look mainly at results. Rule consequentialism looks at which rules would lead to the best results if people accepted and learned them.
A rule can be useful even when following it does not create the best result in one unusual case.
Rules against harming innocent people, stealing, lying, and breaking promises may help create trust and safety.
The theory must consider teaching rules, learning them, imperfect rule-following, and responses such as punishment.
Philosophers disagree about what counts as a good result: happiness, fulfilled desires, knowledge, friendship, fairness, or other goods may matter.
summaries.why_it_matters: This theory helps us see why moral life may need dependable shared rules rather than a fresh calculation every time. It also shows that good intentions are not the only issue: we should think about trust, learning, fairness, mistakes, and long-term effects. Studying it gives us a careful way to compare rules and to ask whether a rule works well for a whole community.

important_terms.definition: A moral idea that judges choices by the results they produce.
A theory that chooses moral rules because accepting those rules is expected to lead to the best results.
How well people’s lives are going, including benefits and harms.
A general guide for what people should or should not do.
A result that is better or worse than another result.

questions_to_think_about: Should a good rule have exceptions, or can too many exceptions make it confusing?
Is it fair to judge every person’s benefit in exactly the same way?
When might breaking a usual rule prevent a disaster?
Should a rule be chosen for what actually happens or for what we can reasonably expect to happen?

summaries.example: Suppose a city is deciding between two public codes. Code A says that officials must never reveal private information. Code B adds many detailed exceptions whenever disclosure might produce slightly more good. Rule consequentialists would compare not only the immediate results of each disclosure policy but also the effects of public acceptance: trust in officials, temptation to misuse exceptions, clarity for citizens, and the cost of teaching the code. They might favor a simpler confidentiality rule with a carefully understood emergency provision, even though an act-by-act calculation could sometimes recommend disclosure for a small gain.
summaries.summary:
Rule consequentialism belongs to the consequentialist family, but it evaluates moral rules rather than treating each decision as an isolated optimization problem. Full rule consequentialism says that rules are selected solely by the goodness of their consequences and that these rules determine which kinds of acts are wrong. It also applies rule-based consequentialist standards to practical deliberation and to sanctions such as blame, guilt, praise, and punishment. This distinguishes it from partial rule consequentialism, which may use rules for decision-making while retaining an act-consequentialist standard of wrongness. It also differs from global consequentialism, which evaluates acts, rules, motives, procedures, and sanctions directly by their own consequences.

The account of what is good remains controversial. Utilitarian approaches aggregate welfare, but welfare may be understood hedonistically, as pleasure minus pain, or through desire fulfillment and broader goods. Nonutilitarian consequentialists may include justice, fairness, equality, rights, or desert, although simply declaring these valuable does not explain them. Prioritarianism gives extra weight to gains for people who are worse off, but faces questions about how to set the weights and whether this conflicts with impartiality.

Rule consequentialism must also be formulated precisely. It may concern actual or expected value; compliance or acceptance; complete acceptance or acceptance by a large majority; or the teaching of a code to future generations. Acceptance has effects beyond behavior, including assurance, incentives, deterrence, and public trust. key_ideas: Rule consequentialism separates the selection of rules from the direct assessment of individual acts. This can preserve trust, reduce calculation errors, and avoid biased or rushed judgments.
Full rule consequentialism applies consequence-based rules not only to wrongness but also to moral decision procedures and sanctions such as blame and punishment.

The theory’s account of value is unsettled. Welfare may involve pleasure and pain, desire fulfillment, or objective goods such as knowledge, friendship, achievement, and autonomy; justice, fairness, and equality may also matter.
A major formulation question is whether to count compliance with rules, communal acceptance, or the costs and benefits of teaching rules to new generations.
Because acceptance will be incomplete, the theory must include rules for enforcement and punishment. A code designed for perfect compliance would have little reason to contain punishment rules.

Critics argue that rule consequentialism either collapses into act consequentialism or irrationally sticks to rules. Supporters answer that simple, teachable, non-demanding rules can have better overall effects than endlessly amended rules.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rule consequentialism connects moral theory with the design of public moral practices. It asks not only, “What would help most in this case?” but also, “What rules could people learn, trust, and use without bias, confusion, or destructive incentives?” That makes the theory relevant to questions about law, education, institutions, punishment, and social cooperation. Its debates also clarify a central issue in ethics: whether moral justification should focus on outcomes, stable principles, fairness, or some combination of these.

important_terms.definition: A form of consequentialism that evaluates acts, rules, practices, or institutions solely by the goodness of their consequences.
The view that acts are wrong when forbidden by rules selected because their acceptance, teaching, or related effects would have the best expected consequences.
The view that an act is wrong when it produces less good than an available alternative, regardless of whether a general rule forbids it.
The total welfare or well-being produced across people, treating equal-sized benefits and harms to different people equally in the basic calculation.
The view that rules should be assessed using rational estimates of possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities, rather than by inaccessible actual outcomes alone.
A consequentialist view that assesses everything, including acts, rules, decisions, and sanctions, directly by its own consequences.
A view that gives greater weight to an equal-sized welfare gain when it helps someone who is worse off.
The idea that a moral code should be suitable for being openly taught and known, rather than depending on secret principles.

questions_to_think_about: Does a rule’s justification depend more on its actual consequences or on the consequences that could reasonably be expected?
Can a moral theory consistently require a rule that sometimes fails to maximize the good in an individual case?
Should equality be valued independently, or can concern for the worse off arise from welfare considerations alone?
Is a code chosen for new generations less culturally relative than one assessed from an existing society’s accepted rules?
How should a theory balance simple rules, emergency exceptions, and the danger of excessive self-sacrifice?

summaries.example: A student council is choosing a rule about promises. One proposal says, “Keep every promise, no matter what.” Another says, “Keep promises unless breaking one is needed to stop a serious harm.” A third says, “Break a promise whenever it seems to help a little more.” A rule consequentialist would ask which rule, if widely accepted, would create the most trust and good results. The first rule may be too strict, the third may make promises unreliable, and the second may work better if its emergency exception is clear and not too easy to abuse.
summaries.summary:
Rule consequentialism is a theory about how consequences can justify moral rules. Consequentialist theories judge acts, traits, practices, or institutions by their results. Utilitarian versions usually calculate aggregate welfare, meaning the combined benefits and harms of all affected people. But philosophers disagree about welfare: it might involve pleasure and the absence of pain, fulfilled desires, or goods such as knowledge, friendship, achievement, and autonomy. Some consequentialists also discuss justice, fairness, equality, rights, and desert, though a theory must explain these ideas rather than merely add them to a list of goals.

Full rule consequentialism says that an act is wrong when it is forbidden by rules justified by their consequences. It also says that people should normally make decisions through such rules and that rules should determine when praise, blame, guilt, or punishment are appropriate. This is broader than partial rule consequentialism, which may use consequence-based rules for decision-making while judging wrongness directly by acts. Global consequentialism goes further by assessing every relevant feature directly, including rules and sanctions.

The details matter. A code may be judged by actual results or expected results, and by compliance, acceptance, or teaching. Acceptance can create trust, reassurance, incentives, and deterrence. Teaching rules has costs, especially when rules are complicated or demanding, so the best code may not be the one with the most exceptions or the strongest demand for sacrifice. A code also must allow for incomplete acceptance: some people will misunderstand, resist, or fail to be motivated by it. key_ideas: Rule consequentialism chooses rules by their overall effects, especially when a community accepts and teaches them.
It differs from act consequentialism: a rule consequentialist may support a rule even when breaking it would produce slightly more good in one case.
Full rule consequentialism covers three questions: which acts are wrong, how people should decide, and when blame or punishment is appropriate.
There are disagreements about what counts as welfare and whether other values, such as justice, fairness, or equality, should also be promoted.
Rules need to be understandable and teachable. Too many exceptions can create confusion, temptation, and less trust.
Since people will not all accept or follow the same code perfectly, the theory must include ways to respond to mistakes, danger, and rule-breaking.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory matters because shared rules shape more than individual choices. They influence whether people trust one another, whether institutions are predictable, how children learn moral ideas, and whether punishment protects people or merely expresses anger. Rule consequentialism also gives a structured way to examine disagreements about welfare, equality, emergencies, and the limits of moral demands. Even if one rejects the theory, its distinctions help explain why a good immediate result may not justify a rule that damages trust over time.

important_terms.definition: A moral theory that evaluates choices mainly or entirely by the goodness of their results.
The view that the best moral rules are those whose acceptance or teaching would lead to the best overall results.
The view that each act should be judged directly by whether another available act would have produced a better result.
The total amount of well-being after benefits and harms to different people are added together.
The good or bad that follows from an action, rule, or practice.
The effects of people accepting a rule, including trust and incentives, not just the effects of obeying it.
A theory that gives more importance to helping people who are worse off, while still comparing overall welfare.
A moral code that can be openly taught and known by the people who are expected to follow it.

questions_to_think_about: Would people trust promises if everyone could break them whenever they predicted a small benefit?
Should a moral rule be based on what really happens or on what people have good reasons to expect?
Can a simple rule be better overall than a more accurate but complicated rule?
Does treating everyone equally always require equal outcomes?
When, if ever, should preventing a disaster override an ordinary rule?
